newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe to maintain controversial anti-migrant bill.
newsitem.headline: Juppe to maintain controversial anti-migrant bill.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe will maintain a controversial draft anti-immigration bill despite mounting opposition from intellectuals, his office said on Saturday.
"The government will maintain the text as it stands," a Juppe spokeswoman told Reuters.

She was commenting on a statement on Friday by Guy Sorman, an author who is an occasional consultant to Juppe, who told French television the premier was opposed to an especially controversial part of the bill tabled before parliament by hardline Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre.
The controversial article would require people who supply certificates to foreigners saying they will take responsibility for them during their stay in France to also declare when their guests leave.

Would-be visitors from many Third World countries who cannot show they have enough money to fund a long visit to France are currently granted visas only if they can provide a certificate showing someone in France will provide them with lodging.

The new article, like the certificates before them, are aimed at discouraging would-be illegal immigrants of which there are an estimated one million in France. There are a further four million foreigners legally resident in the country.

But requiring individuals to report to police that their guests had left has raised a storm of protest among intellectuals, painters, doctors and psychiatrists who all flocked on Friday to back a film-maker's appeal for civil disobedience.
The movement reflected concern among intellectuals that the government had copied the far-right, anti-immigration National Front in drafting the bill.
The protest snowballed in just a few days since the Front, which wants to expel millions of foreigners, took a fourth southern town in a municipal election.
Writers, theatre directors and actors signed the appeal on Thursday and were joined by academics, journalists, lawyers, painters, and sculptors among others on Friday.
But one prominent intellectual, philosopher Alain Finkielkraut, although opposed to the new law, said he believed the petitions would have a counter-effect.
He said the phenomenon of the privileged few, living in areas where there were no poor immigrants, telling the lower classes what to think would have exactly the opposite effect to the desired one.
He was backed by leftist newsmagazine editor Jean Daniel who wrote that "the anti-racist pleas have so far only resulted in creating more racists."

Public opinion polls have shown that the vast majority of the French public, including many people opposed to Le Pen, favoured measures to curb illegal immigration, which is widely seen as being responsible for rising unemployment and delinquency.
